title: Why Threatening Consequences Causes Misbehavior
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin observes that threatening consequences instead of enforcing them has become more common since the pandemic, driven by pressure to give students more chances and a generational discomfort with setting firm limits. He argues threats reliably backfire through five mechanisms: they signal fear rather than authority, they teach students that the teacher's words carry no weight, they eventually provoke direct challenge and aggression when a teacher finally tries to enforce something, they invite laughter and immaturity once students realize threats are empty, and over time they turn teachers into angrier, more bitter versions of themselves as frustration accumulates. His alternative is a genuine, promised warning issued in the exact manner modeled to students on a first infraction, which he says carries real power because it is backed by a real consequence, unlike an empty threat.
points: Threatening rather than enforcing consequences has become more common since the pandemic, driven by pressure for leniency and generational discomfort with limits.
Threats signal fear, teaching students the teacher can be ignored, manipulated, and not taken seriously.
Empty threats eventually provoke direct challenge and aggression once a teacher tries to actually enforce something.
Repeated empty threats invite laughter and immaturity, undermining the teacher's authority further.
The alternative is a real, pre-modeled warning backed by an actual consequence, which carries genuine power unlike a threat.
quotes: The truth is, it doesn’t matter what you think or believe, the failure to follow through with a predetermined consequence the moment you witness misbehavior will always and eventually result in more misbehavior.
The first time you threaten action, rather than acting, you communicate loud and clear to your students that you’re afraid to follow through.
Without real consequence, threats will eventually be met with laughter. Your students will see you as insignificant, no more a leader than a hanger-on friend.
In the face of daily chaos, teachers eventually become who they despise.
Threats by their nature mean nothing. Forgotten sound lost in the wind. They have no teeth, no bite, no meaning of any kind.
A warning, on the other hand, given in the exact manner modeled and promised to students, and in response to a first infraction of classroom rules, matters.
